senses: A light railroad car propelled by a hand-operated pumping mechanism
examples: A small handcar rested on the tracks, its iron pump waiting for a human touch to animate it.

senses: A type of salumi made by curing strips of fatback with rosemary and other herbs and spices.
ety: Borrowed from Italian lardo. Doublet of lard.

senses: Splitting into fibrils or fibres.
Of a muscle, especially in the heart: undergoing fibrillation; quivering.
examples: A publicity plane flew along the Croisette, its pennant fluttering like the trace of a fibrillating heart, unnoticed by the sunbathers stretched in their loungers in the hotel concessions.

senses: Like or resembling a raptor; seizing or plundering, like a bird of prey.
examples: When its legs are extended, it measures one and a half inches wide, and the raptorial claws hint that it is a fierce predator.

senses: An insidious reach or influence.
Something like a zoological limb.
ety: From New Latin tentāculum, from tentō. Doublet of tentaculum.

senses: The study of parasites.
A member of a crew, especially the crew of a ship.
examples: Next year this service is to be operated entirely by automatic control, though the trains will carry at least one crewman.

senses: An artistic movement and an aesthetic philosophy that aims for the liberation of the mind by emphasizing the critical and imaginative powers of the subconscious.
Art with a surreal aesthetic or narrative, regardless of whether or not it is linked to the surrealist movement.
ety: Borrowed from French surréalisme. By surface analysis, sur- + realism or surreal + -ism.

senses: A (variety of) citrus drink made from water, sugar, and the juice of limes.
A serving of this drink.
A type of two-ply carpet.
ety: From Kidderminster, the English town where they were once manufactured.

senses: A fine semi-lustrous crepe in satin weave.
examples: Her exquisite figure was enhanced by a wonderful gown of indigo charmeuse.

senses: An injunction.
ety: From Middle English entrediten, from Old French entredire (“forbid”), from Latin interdīcō (“prohibit, forbid”), from inter- (“between”) + dīcō (“say”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-.

senses: Catachresis for dowdy.
ety: The adjective is derived from Middle English doughty (“brave, bold, valiant”), from Old English dohtiġ, dyhtiġ (“competent, good, strong, valiant”), from Proto-West Germanic *duhtīg. The English word may be analysed as dought + -y, and is cognate with Scots douchty, douchtie (“bold, valiant”), Dutch duchtig (“severe, strict”), German tüchtig (“capable, competent, efficient; big; hard”), Danish dygtig (“virtuous, proficient”), Swedish duktig (“efficient; good; capable, clever, smart”), Icelandic dygðugur (“virtuous, stable”). The noun is derived from the adjective.

senses: A politician.
examples: I think politics attracts a particular type of person – and I don′t think I′m one of those. The pollies certainly need to be very dedicated and to be prepared to invest huge amounts of their time.
On another surveillance flight I accompanied a prominent pollie of the day, a big, bluff, ruddy-faced Minister.

senses: A member of a habitation colony at Stadacona founded by Samuel de Champlain, where Quebec City now lies.
A play in the form of a monologue
sad, mournful
ety: Borrowed from Italian mesto and used as a tempo mark.

senses: Hitherto unoccupied “living space” claimed as one’s rightful domain.
A masterless samurai (who often becomes a mercenary to make ends meet).
ety: From Japanese 浪人 (rōnin), in turn from Middle Chinese 浪人 (MC langH nyin, “dissolute, wasteful, unrestrained + person”).
examples: Back at Asano’s home in Ako, his chancellor, Oishi (Tatsuo Ichikawa), rallies the samurai, now known as ronin because they are without a master, in a campaign to avenge Asano and restore his clan’s honor.

senses: A type of Sicilian sesame bread.
A type of sandwich, typically made in New Orleans and containing layers of olive salad, mozzarella and meats, made using that bread.
A kind of olive salad made with giardiniera.
ety: From Sicilian, diminutive of muffe (“mold, mushroom”), perhaps due to the appearance of the round sandwich bread being reminiscent of a mushroom cap.

senses: Synonym of jambul.
Like a chimera.
Imaginary, fanciful.
The state of being animate (alive or supernaturally seeming alive).
examples: These may differ radically in their linguistic animacy, as briefly discussed above, without this having any consequences for their biological animacy.

senses: Within the trachea
A stripping or plundering; spoliation.
An artistic movement of the first decade of the 20th century which emphasized spontaneity and the use of extremely bright colors.
ety: From French fauvisme, attributed to French art critic Louis Vauxcelles.

senses: of, related to or affected with monophasia
having a single phase
Having been mussed: messy, rumpled.
Resembling typhoid.
Of or having somewhat of a purple color or hue.
A person whose mother tongue is one other than that spoken by the majority.
An ancient Irish public national assembly called upon the death of a king, queen, notable sage or warrior as part of ancestor-worship practices.
ety: From Irish aonach, from Old Irish óenach, from óen (“one”).

senses: A person who has been evacuated, especially a civilian evacuated from a dangerous place in time of war
ety: From French évacué, évacuée, from évacuer, equivalent to evacu(ate) + -ee.

senses: Having a (specified form of) mane.
The cavity of the skull in which the brain is contained.
A Chinese state-run socialist work cooperative, institution, organisation or government department
ety: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of the Mandarin Chinese pronunciation for 單位／单位 (dānwèi).

senses: One who, or that which, deletes.
Coated in shellac.
examples: At Boy Bar, the bouncers, two tall, emaciated young men with shellacked hair under their bowler hats, were standing just inside the door to escape the cold.

senses: To rub or wear off; erode.
To wear down or exhaust, as a person; irritate.
To irritate by rubbing; chafe.
To cause the surface to become more rough.
To undergo abrasion.
ety: From Latin abrādō (“scrape off”), from ab (“from, away from”) + rādō (“scrape”). First attested in 1677.

senses: All those areas of the Earth where the surface is frozen.
examples: Climate change has a strong effect on the cryosphere.
